Name: Janus (Ianus)
Description: Janus is the Roman god of beginnings, thresholds, gates, and transitions, commonly represented with two faces looking in opposite directions. Roman ritual regularly placed him at the opening of actions and ceremonies, and the month of January was associated with him. The Ianus Geminus in Rome was famously described as open in wartime and closed in peace. Later antiquarian tradition also made Janus a primordial king or civilizer who received Saturn in Latium. As a symbolic figure he joins past and future, inside and outside, and the ordered passage from one state into another.

Name: Venus
Description: Venus is the Roman goddess of sexual attraction, fertility, beauty, and generative power, whose cult acquired major civic and dynastic roles. As Venus Genetrix she was honored as the mother of Aeneas and ancestral protectress of the Julian line; Venus Victrix linked her favor with victory, while Venus Erycina represented an important cult with Sicilian and Mediterranean connections. Under the late Republic and Empire these forms allowed erotic, familial, military, and political meanings to converge in a goddess who could symbolize both personal desire and the flourishing continuity of the Roman people.

Name: Saturn (Saturnus)
Description: Saturn is an old Roman agricultural deity associated especially with sowing and with the mythic Golden Age. Later Roman tradition portrayed him as an exiled ruler who came to Latium, sometimes as the guest or partner of Janus, and taught an earlier, more abundant way of life. At Saturnalia his normally bound cult image was ritually released, while feasting, gift-giving, gaming, and temporary reversals of social convention evoked an age of freedom and plenty. His temple in the Forum also housed the state treasury, linking an agrarian god of stored abundance with the material resources of the Roman state.

Name: Jupiter (Iuppiter)
Description: Jupiter is Rome’s sovereign sky god and the principal divine guarantor of oaths, treaties, victory, and public authority. As Iuppiter Optimus Maximus he presided from the Capitoline temple, where victorious generals completed triumphal vows and the state cultivated one of its most important public cults. Thunder and lightning were read as signs of his will, and forms such as Jupiter Stator, Victor, and Feretrius connected him with the preservation and success of Rome in war. Together with Juno and Minerva he formed the Capitoline Triad, making Jupiter a central link between divine sovereignty, lawful order, and the Roman state.

Name: Mars
Description: Mars is Rome’s major god of war and one of the central deities of the Roman state, while older ritual associations also connect him with fields, livestock, boundaries, and the protection of the community. March, the month named for him, opened the traditional campaigning season and was marked by ceremonies involving the Salii and their sacred shields. Other rites associated with his martial sphere included the Equirria, the Armilustrium, and the October Horse. As the divine father of Romulus in Rome’s founding legend, Mars joins agricultural protection, disciplined violence, and the expansion of the civic community.

Name: Faunus
Description: Faunus is an old Italian rural deity associated with woods, fields, flocks, fertility, and prophecy. Ancient tradition describes prophetic voices heard in groves and dream-oracles received at his sacred places. Under Greek influence he was identified with Pan, while Roman authors also associated him in varying ways with figures such as Lupercus. In later mythic genealogies Faunus could appear as an ancient king of Latium, making him both a rustic divine power and a bridge between wild landscape, prophecy, and legendary Latin kingship.

Name: Evander
Description: Evander is the Arcadian culture-hero whom Roman tradition placed at Pallantium on the future Palatine Hill before the arrival of Aeneas. In the Aeneid he is an elderly local king who welcomes Aeneas and becomes his ally, while other traditions credit him and his people with bringing Greek rites, letters, and customs into early Italy. He is especially associated with the Roman cult of Hercules at the Ara Maxima and is remembered as the father of Pallas. In Roman foundation myth, Evander functions as a civilizing bridge between the Greek world and the pre-Roman landscape of Latium.

Name: Tiberinus
Description: Tiberinus is the divine personification of the Tiber River, one of the sacred powers most closely tied to Rome’s landscape and foundation traditions. In Virgil’s Aeneid he appears to Aeneas in a dream, assures him that he has reached his destined land, and directs him toward an alliance with Evander. Roman legend also connected the river with the survival of Romulus and Remus and with an Alban king named Tiberinus who was said to have drowned in the river and given it his name. As a river god he embodies the Tiber as boundary, route, source of fertility, and dangerous but indispensable lifeline of Rome.

Name: Hercules
Description: Hercules entered Roman religion as a powerful civilizing hero whose strength could protect travel, exchange, and communal order. Roman tradition located his defeat of the cattle-stealing Cacus near the future Forum Boarium and connected the episode with the Ara Maxima, one of Rome’s oldest and most prestigious Herculean cult sites. His Roman forms, including Hercules Invictus, emphasized victory, endurance, vows, and reciprocal offering. The cult’s strong presence near the Tiber riverfront helped make Hercules a heroic guardian of a zone where trade, transport, sacrifice, and foundation legend converged.

Name: Latinus
Description: Latinus is the legendary king of the Latins who receives Aeneas after the Trojans reach Latium. In Virgil and other Roman traditions, omens and dynastic expectations lead him toward alliance with Aeneas and the marriage of his daughter Lavinia, although the settlement is contested by Turnus and his supporters. As a mythic eponym and ancestral king, Latinus personifies the native Latin side of Rome’s foundation story and helps transform the arrival of outsiders into a legitimate local dynasty. His royal center, Laurentum, was traditionally placed on the coast between Ostia and Lavinium; its precise archaeological location remains uncertain, generally in the Castel Porziano–Tor Paterno area.

Name: Aeneas
Description: Aeneas is Rome’s Trojan ancestral hero, defined above all by pietas: duty toward gods, family, and destiny. Roman tradition tells how he escaped the fall of Troy with his father Anchises and the household gods, wandered through the Mediterranean, descended to the underworld, and eventually reached Latium. There he allied with Latinus, married Lavinia, fought Turnus, and became associated with the foundation of Lavinium and the line leading through Alba Longa to Rome. In Roman literature and political memory, Aeneas embodies the transfer of Trojan sacred identity into an Italian and ultimately Roman future.

Name: Quirinus
Description: Quirinus is an archaic Roman deity with an old cult on the Quirinal Hill and one of Rome’s major priesthoods. By the late Republic he was firmly identified with Romulus after the founder’s apotheosis, but the god appears to have had an earlier identity independent of that equation. Ancient and modern interpretations connect Quirinus with the Roman citizen body, the Quirites, and with the settled civic community as distinct from Mars’s more overtly martial sphere. In Rome’s later foundation narrative he therefore became the divine form of Romulus and a symbol of the founder transformed from warrior-king into guardian of the organized citizen state.

Name: Romulus
Description: Romulus is the legendary founder and first king of Rome and the twin brother of Remus. Roman tradition tells how the twins survived exposure beside the Tiber, were suckled by a she-wolf, restored their grandfather Numitor at Alba Longa, and then set out to found a new city. The brothers quarreled over the foundation, and in the best-known version Romulus or one of his followers killed Remus after he crossed the new walls. Tradition dated Rome’s foundation to 753 BCE and credited Romulus with organizing the Senate, the army, and the early citizen body, as well as with the conflict and eventual union with the Sabines. His mysterious disappearance was later interpreted as apotheosis, identifying him with Quirinus.

Name: Numa Pompilius
Description: Numa Pompilius is the legendary second king of Rome, traditionally a Sabine chosen to succeed Romulus. Roman authors portrayed his reign as the peaceful counterpart to Romulus’s wars and credited him with organizing major priesthoods, cults, ritual rules, and reforms of the calendar. Tradition also linked him with the nymph Egeria, whose divine counsel sanctioned his religious legislation, and claimed that the doors of Janus remained closed during his reign. The institutional details attributed to Numa are difficult to assign historically to a single ruler, but the figure became Rome’s archetypal priest-king and lawgiver.

Name: Egeria
Description: Egeria is a Roman nymph associated with a sacred grove and spring outside the Porta Capena. In tradition she is the divine counselor and sometimes consort of Numa Pompilius, instructing the king in ritual and law and thereby giving sacred authority to Rome’s early religious institutions. She was also connected with water, childbirth, and prophetic inspiration. Egeria’s role in the Numa cycle makes her a mediating figure through whom natural sacred space, divine knowledge, and royal legislation are joined.

Name: Tullus Hostilius
Description: Tullus Hostilius is the legendary third king of Rome, portrayed by Roman historians as a warrior-king in deliberate contrast with the peaceful Numa. Tradition credits him with war against Alba Longa, famously resolved through the combat of the Horatii and Curiatii, followed by Alba’s destruction and the transfer of many of its inhabitants to Rome. Later stories also associate his reign with fighting against Fidenae and Veii. His death was moralized as a warning against neglect of ritual: after attempting religious rites incorrectly, he and his house were said to have been destroyed by Jupiter’s lightning.

Name: Ancus Marcius
Description: Ancus Marcius is the legendary fourth king of Rome and was said to be a descendant of Numa Pompilius. Roman tradition presents him as combining Numa-like religious concern with military expansion, crediting him with renewed ritual procedures for declaring war, campaigns against Latin communities, and the incorporation of conquered populations into Rome. He was also traditionally credited with the Pons Sublicius, saltworks near the Tiber mouth, a prison, and the foundation of Ostia. Archaeology does not support a seventh-century city at Ostia—the earliest securely identified urban fortification there belongs to the fourth century BCE—so these works are best treated as parts of Rome’s later royal tradition rather than secure contemporary achievements.

Name: Tarquinius Priscus
Description: Tarquinius Priscus is the legendary fifth king of Rome, said to have come from the Etruscan city of Tarquinii with his wife Tanaquil. Roman tradition describes his accession after Ancus Marcius and credits him with military successes, enlargement of the Senate and cavalry, and major public works associated with the Circus Maximus, drainage of the Forum area, and the beginnings of the Capitoline temple of Jupiter. His reign represents the strong Etruscan dimension of early Rome in later historical memory. According to the traditional narrative he was assassinated by sons of Ancus, after which Tanaquil helped secure the succession of Servius Tullius.

Name: Servius Tullius
Description: Servius Tullius is the legendary sixth king of Rome, remembered above all as a political and military organizer. Tradition gives him an unusual rise from humble or servile origins under the protection of Tanaquil and credits him with the census, wealth-based military classes and centuries, and institutions later associated with the comitia centuriata. He was also linked with the Aventine cult of Diana and with the expansion of Rome’s defenses. The surviving wall conventionally called the “Servian Wall” is largely a fourth-century BCE construction, much later than the traditional reign, so the association of Servius with that masonry should not be taken literally. His death at the hands of Tarquinius Superbus and Tullia became a central prelude to the fall of the monarchy.

Name: Lucius Junius Brutus
Description: Lucius Junius Brutus is the semi-legendary Roman figure traditionally credited with leading the overthrow of Tarquinius Superbus and helping establish the Republic in 509 BCE. Later accounts make him a relative of the Tarquinian house who survived the king’s suspicion by feigning stupidity. After Lucretia’s rape and suicide he is said to have sworn an oath against monarchy, rallied the revolt, and become one of Rome’s first consuls. The story that he ordered the execution of his own sons for joining a royalist conspiracy made him an emblem of civic duty placed above family. Tradition has him die later in 509 BCE in single combat with Arruns Tarquinius at the Battle of Silva Arsia.

Name: Tarquinius Superbus
Description: Tarquinius Superbus is the legendary seventh and last king of Rome, remembered by Roman authors as the model of tyrannical kingship. Tradition says that he seized power after the murder of Servius Tullius, marginalized the Senate, ruled through fear, and compelled major public works while also completing or advancing monuments associated with the Capitoline temple and Rome’s drainage system. The rape of Lucretia by his son Sextus became the immediate narrative trigger for the revolt that expelled the Tarquins in 509 BCE. Tarquinius then sought restoration with outside allies but failed and, according to Roman tradition, eventually died in exile at Cumae around 495 BCE.

Name: Sextus Tarquinius
Description: Sextus Tarquinius is the legendary son of Rome’s last king, Tarquinius Superbus. Roman tradition first makes him central to the capture of Gabii, where he allegedly pretended to defect and then undermined the city from within on his father’s instructions. He is most infamous for the rape of Lucretia, whose subsequent suicide became the immediate catalyst in the traditional story of the monarchy’s overthrow in 509 BCE. After the Tarquins were expelled, Sextus fled Rome and was reportedly killed at Gabii. In Roman memory he became a concentrated symbol of the violence and corruption attributed to the last royal house.

Name: Lucretia
Description: Lucretia is the legendary Roman noblewoman whose rape by Sextus Tarquinius and subsequent suicide stand at the center of Rome’s traditional account of the fall of the monarchy. Wife of Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, she was celebrated by later Roman writers as an exemplary matron. In the story she disclosed the assault to her family, demanded vengeance, and then killed herself; Brutus used the outrage surrounding her death to rally resistance against the Tarquins. Her narrative became a powerful Roman symbol of violated household honor, resistance to tyranny, and the moral drama attached to the Republic’s foundation.

Name: Mucius Scaevola (Gaius Mucius)
Description: Gaius Mucius Scaevola is a legendary hero of the early Republic associated with Rome’s struggle against the Etruscan king Lars Porsenna. According to Livy, Mucius entered the enemy camp intending to assassinate Porsenna but killed the wrong man and was captured. He then placed his right hand into a fire to demonstrate Roman contempt for pain and claimed that three hundred other young Romans were prepared to attempt the same mission. Porsenna released him, and Mucius received the surname Scaevola, “left-handed.” The tale became an enduring exemplum of courage, endurance, and self-sacrifice for the Republic.

Name: Horatius Cocles
Description: Horatius Cocles is a legendary Roman soldier associated with Lars Porsenna’s attack on Rome after the expulsion of the Tarquins. In the best-known version he and a small number of companions held the Pons Sublicius while Romans behind them destroyed the bridge, after which Horatius continued the defense alone and escaped by entering the Tiber. Ancient versions differ in details of his survival and injuries, while the historicity of the episode cannot be established. Roman tradition nevertheless made Horatius a model of individual courage used to protect the entire civic community.

Name: Camillus (Marcus Furius Camillus)
Description: Marcus Furius Camillus was a historical Roman general and statesman of the early fourth century BCE, later celebrated as a “second founder of Rome.” He captured Veii in 396 BCE and subsequently withdrew to Ardea while facing prosecution over the distribution of spoils and related political accusations. When Gauls sacked Rome in the early fourth century BCE, later Roman tradition made Camillus the returning savior who rejected the ransom and drove them out; the dramatic details of that rescue are not securely historical. He nevertheless held repeated high commands, including five dictatorships in the traditional record, and remained an important figure in wars against neighboring peoples. His later image fused a real Republican commander with an exemplary narrative of Roman recovery and resilience.

Name: Marcus Curtius
Description: Marcus Curtius is a legendary Roman youth associated with the Lacus Curtius in the Forum. In Livy’s best-known version, a chasm opened in 362 BCE and diviners declared that Rome must sacrifice what constituted its greatest strength. Curtius answered that Rome’s true wealth was the courage of its citizens and soldiers, then rode fully armed into the gulf, which closed over him. The story is one of several ancient explanations for the name of the Lacus Curtius and became a compact exemplum of devotion to the commonwealth through voluntary self-sacrifice.

Name: Peter the Apostle
Description: Peter the Apostle, also called Simon or Cephas, was a Galilean fisherman and one of the earliest and most prominent followers of Jesus. The Gospel of John associates Peter and Andrew with Bethsaida, while the Synoptic tradition places Peter’s household at Capernaum; the precise archaeological location of ancient Bethsaida remains debated. The New Testament portrays Peter as both an impetuous disciple and a major leader in the Jerusalem movement, and Paul’s letters independently attest Cephas as an important early Christian figure. Early Christian tradition places Peter’s final ministry and martyrdom at Rome under Nero, probably in the 60s CE; crucifixion is early tradition, while the familiar detail that he was crucified upside down is later. In Christian memory he became the archetypal apostolic shepherd and “rock” of the community.

Name: Paul the Apostle
Description: Paul the Apostle, born Saul and associated with Tarsus in Cilicia, was a Jewish follower of Jesus whose letters are among the earliest surviving Christian writings. He describes himself as a former persecutor of the church who experienced a revelation of Christ and then became a missionary, especially among non-Jews. Paul founded or corresponded with communities across Asia Minor and Greece and articulated influential teachings on faith, grace, resurrection, and the incorporation of Gentiles. His letters also record a sharp dispute with Cephas/Peter at Antioch over table fellowship and relations between Jewish and Gentile believers. Acts presents Paul as a Roman citizen, and early Christian tradition places his martyrdom at Rome under Nero in the mid-to-late 60s CE.

Name: Celsus
Description: Celsus was a late second-century Middle Platonist philosopher and one of the earliest substantial pagan critics of Christianity. His polemic, usually called the True Doctrine or True Word, was probably written around 175–181 CE and survives only through quotations and paraphrases in Origen’s much later Contra Celsum. Celsus attacked Christian claims about revelation, scripture, Jesus, resurrection, and the rejection of traditional cult, and he urged Christians to participate in the civic and imperial order. Almost nothing secure is known about his biography, birthplace, or lifespan; the dates and Roman location used here should therefore be understood as approximate visualization choices anchored to his late-second-century activity.

Name: Ennius
Description: Quintus Ennius, born at Rudiae in southern Italy around 239 BCE, became one of the foundational figures of Latin literature. Ancient tradition remembered him as multilingual in Greek, Latin, and Oscan—the source of his famous claim to possess “three hearts.” His Annales narrated Roman history in Greek-style hexameter and profoundly influenced later Roman epic, while he also wrote tragedies, satires, and other works now surviving largely in fragments. Later Romans treated Ennius as a poetic ancestor and cultural mediator who helped give Latin literature the forms and ambitions of the Greek tradition.
